public_rationale: He says flatly that AI has no return on investment. Some of the record backs him. Bain's April 2026 survey, which he cites, found that nearly 40% of firms that measured savings landed at 10% or less, against higher targets. Bain sums it up as 'The value didn't arrive.' PwC data reported by Fortune say 56% of companies get nothing from AI yet. But the absolute claim does not hold. The same Bain study reports a meaningful group of firms whose targeted savings actually materialized. Wharton's 2025 survey found three in four enterprise leaders see positive returns on generative AI, and 72% formally measure ROI. So returns are uneven and often below expectations, but the evidence does not show there is no ROI at all.
limitations: Evidence on both sides is mostly self-reported executive surveys.
Cost savings reported in surveys are not always net of full AI costs.
'AI' scope (LLMs vs all AI) is not fixed by the speaker.

from_speaker: nobody can show you the ROI from AI

our_interpretation: Plain reading: spending on AI (mainly LLMs and generative AI, given the context) does not yield measurable returns. Credible measured or reported positive returns would count against it. Widespread failure to realize returns would count in its favor.
He names no period for this ongoing state. I use January 2025 to the post date (2 June 2026), the span of the main enterprise ROI surveys before the post. It is not limited to one quarter.
Self-reported executive surveys count as evidence, but they are weaker than audited figures.
criteria.support_condition: Credible studies or disclosures show that firms deploying AI generally fail to get returns that exceed costs, and none can document positive returns.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible studies or company disclosures document positive returns from AI investments for a meaningful share of firms.
